title: Setting the record straight, Euryapteryx moa (Aves: Dinornithiformes) existed in the South Island of New Zealand long before 17 000 years ago
content: It is clear to all students of moa taxonomy that the species are highly variable. Building on Cracraft’s (1976) insights that sexual dimorphism explained much of the observed size variation, I have long advocated the three-dimensional approach of using latitude, altitude, and temporal variation to explaining observed morphological variation in moa species (e.g. Worthy 1987). With the subsequent inclusion of molecular data in the analysis of moa species delimitation, the great extent of intraspecific size variation became well known. This is perhaps best exemplified by extensive data for Dinornis, wherein size variation due to the combination of reversed sexual dimorphism and temperature- or resource-driven size variation along latitudinal, altitudinal, and temporal gradients resulted in the largest size disparity known for any avian species over just a few hundred kilometres in the Holocene (Bunce et al. 2003, Worthy et al. 2005).
siteTitle: Biological Journal of the Linnean Society Current Issue
